The Estate

The door has been open
since 1916.

Neo-Georgian. Four columns. Original 1916 brick — three months were spent sourcing period-accurate replacements when restoration began. Seven fireplaces. 4.15 acres inside the Pinehurst ETJ. Six thousand and seventy-two square feet of living area.

Built by Leonard Tufts' own craftsmen. The same men who built Pinehurst.

"This house needs three or four kids running around."
Walter Hines Page  ·  László portrait  ·  London, 1917
The Man Who Built It

Ambassador. Editor. Visionary.
He named it Garran Hill.

Walter Hines Page was born in Cary, North Carolina, in 1855. He co-founded Doubleday, Page & Co. He edited The Atlantic Monthly. He nominated Woodrow Wilson for the presidency at the 1912 convention.

Wilson appointed him Ambassador to the Court of St. James. He served throughout the First World War — three thousand miles from the house being built for him in his native Moore County.

From London, he wrote home constantly. Not about diplomacy.

"The farm — the farm — the farm."

He purchased the original tract — nearly a thousand acres of timbered land — in February 1913. He named it Garran Hill. Construction was supervised by his son Ralph, following plans from a Boston architectural firm. The craftsmen came from Leonard Tufts' crew — the same men building Pinehurst two miles away.

He returned to North Carolina in December 1918. He died ten days later.

He never spent a night here.
His Words
"Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn't I?"
Walter Hines Page  ·  Aberdeen, NC  ·  December 1918

The Threshold

GARRAN HILL · 1916
inlaid in the brick before ground was broken.

The entry hall opens on original leaded glass sidelights and a herringbone brick floor. White raised-panel wainscoting to chair rail. The brass hardware on every solid-wood door is original. It has not been replaced.

The staircase — mahogany volute — has turned the same curve since 1916.

The Living Room

They made it bigger
so they could dance.

The salon runs nearly forty feet. Tall bare windows parade down both sides. One end anchored by a fireplace. The original proportions were preserved; the room enlarged. Coffered ceiling. Seven carved mantels saved from the original structure, repaired and reset.

It is a room that expects people in it.

The Drawing Room

Fire going.
No one home yet.

Georgian carved mantel. Delft tile surround — blue and white, hand-painted, original. The arch motif that runs through the entire house appears here in the cabinetry, in the doorways, in the fanlights above.

It was specified in 1916. It is still there.

The Dining Room

The shell cabinets were already there
in 1916.

Original frontpiece. Shell cabinets — still there. Butler's arched niche. The handpainted folding screen. The room holds its proportions: 17 feet by 19. It has not been asked to be something else.

The Library

Dead center of the first floor.
Positioned that way in the 2000 plans.

Built-in shelving on three walls. Floor to ceiling. Rolling ladder. French doors to the rear grounds. Brass chandelier. Designed in 2000 to the same standard as the 1916 house it joined.

When you stand in it, you cannot find the seam.

The Kitchen

White cabinetry. Dark granite. Island.
Four windows.

Reclaimed heart-pine floors — the only room in the house that departs from the original oak. Updated in 2000. Two farm sinks. The wall of windows faces an expanse of grass bordered by elder magnolias.

Every morning at 6:30, the deer come through.

The hardware was specified in 1916. It has not been replaced.
The Primary Suite

Designed from scratch in 2000
to match 1916 proportions.

Every component custom-designed. Fifteen architectural drawings document the decisions Thomas O'Shea made. They survive. They transfer with the property.

Three Jacuzzi tubs in the house. The primary balcony — 24 by 11 feet — faces the grounds.

The Powder Room
Fuchsia chinoiserie.
Tennessee marble.

An arched cabinet — the arch motif, consistent through every door and every room since 1916. The brass hardware, original.

4.15 Acres

The world outside these gates
does not exist here.

Low-voltage landscape lighting along the entry drive. Underground utilities throughout. Twenty-eight irrigation zones fed by a 130-foot well. A 20-by-40-foot salt water pool, surrounded by a brick wall with iron gates. Restored in 2022.

The Wee Cottage — complete, self-contained — was moved to the grounds by sky crane.

In 1916, those were saplings. Now they are a forest.
Someone still puts flowers there.
Blue Fox  ·  Betty Dumaine's Irish Hunter  ·  Buried on the Grounds
1959 – 1984

Betty Dumaine kept foxhounds here.
And peacocks. Known to be guard birds.

Elizabeth Dumaine purchased the property in 1959. She was a foxhunter. She added stables, kennels, and an enclosure for peacocks. She changed the name to Hollycrest. She hosted royalty.

Her favorite horse is buried on the grounds.

Blue Fox. Someone still puts flowers there.

"What Ambassador Walter Hines Page started others have continued in a style both innovative and respectful of times when people paid calls, wrote thank-you notes and took Sunday drives."
PineStraw Magazine, October 2019
1999 – 2001

Thomas O'Shea of Durham.
Three years. Every decision documented.

Architect Thomas O'Shea led a complete interior restoration. General contractor: Dennis Dunagan. The interior was gutted. All plumbing and electrical replaced. Custom Marvin windows made to match the 1916 originals. A five-zone climate system engineered specifically to protect the original architecture.

All seven carved mantels saved. Most of the original oak flooring lifted, repaired, and relaid. The period-accurate portico brick took three months to source.

Fifteen architectural drawings survive. They transfer with the property.

It does not feel added. It feels inevitable.

Preservation

A candidate for the National Register
under Criterion B.

The Pines Preservation Guild visited in April 2024. A preservation easement is available: North Carolina tax credit of 25% of fair market value, up to $500,000. Federal income tax deduction potential.

The property qualifies under Criterion B — associated with individuals making significant contributions to history.
